vignette:
Kwame, a 30-year-old African American man, presented to therapy carrying a quiet burden, a weight that had steadily accumulated since the night his life irrevocably shifted. He worked as a curriculum designer, a role that once brought him intellectual satisfaction, now often felt like a stage for his internal struggles. The trauma had occurred over a year ago, when an argument with his then-romantic partner, fueled by alcohol, had escalated into terrifying physical abuse. He vividly recalled the acrid smell of something burning in the kitchen – perhaps food left on the stove in the chaos – mingling with the sharp scent of stale alcohol on his partner’s breath. Amidst the blows, his partner had spat cruel, demeaning remarks about Kwame’s family, words that had cut as deeply as any physical injury.

In the months that followed, Kwame found himself increasingly adrift. The world, once a place he navigated with confidence, now felt fraught with hidden dangers. He noticed that certain sensory inputs had become potent keys to unlock the past. An innocent whiff of alcohol in a public space, or the faint scent of something singed, perhaps from a colleague’s reheated lunch in the office kitchen, would instantly pull him back. These specific triggers, whether the familiar olfactory cues or an offhand comment about someone’s family during a team meeting, weren't just passing annoyances; they were gateways. When these triggers arose, they would plunge him into a full-sensory re-experience of the abuse. He would suddenly feel the phantom ache in his ribs and jaw, the exact same pain as during the event, and the sheer terror he’d felt that night would flood back, leaving him breathless and disoriented, often smelling the burnt food and stale alcohol as if he were there again. Each instance, distinct in its sensory assault, also brought with it a chilling conviction: he was fundamentally changed, a person tainted by the violence, and he would never truly be safe again.

Beyond the visceral recall, these encounters also solidified a profound sense of internal alienation. Each time a trigger led him back to that night, the memory itself reinforced a crushing conviction: the person he had become was unrecognisable to him. The confident, outgoing man he once was seemed to have vanished, replaced by someone constantly on edge. The vivid, painful memories themselves also sharpened his senses to the very cues that had once signaled danger, making him even more prone to being triggered. He found himself scanning his environment for any hint of alcohol or smoke, and bracing himself when colleagues spoke casually about their families, turning everyday interactions into potential minefields.

This constant internal replay, coupled with the frequent re-triggering, fueled a deep-seated sense of injustice. What happened to him was profoundly unfair, he believed, and nothing had been done to truly rectify it. He found himself ruminating endlessly on the unfairness, feeling angry and helpless that his life had been so irrevocably altered without any external resolution. This pervasive sense of injustice, in turn, deepened his feeling of being unrecognisable, as if the trauma had not just affected him, but fundamentally rewritten who he was. Moreover, the lingering memory of the abuse often brought with it a profound sense of contamination. He felt dirty, somehow tainted by what had transpired, as though the physical and emotional violence had left an indelible stain on his very being. This feeling of being soiled made him withdraw further, avoiding social gatherings and even intimate connections, lest he somehow transmit this perceived impurity.

Kwame's professional life, once a source of stability, began to suffer. His concentration wavered, and the creative spark essential for curriculum design dimmed. He found himself increasingly isolated, eating lunch alone and avoiding casual conversations with colleagues to minimize the risk of encountering a family-related comment that might send him spiraling. He knew he needed help when the fear of encountering a trigger began to dictate his entire routine, shrinking his world to a suffocating degree. He came to therapy hoping to reclaim some semblance of his former self, desperate to escape the tightening grip of his past and the constant feeling that he was a stranger in his own skin.
